facts.text: Krull cost a reported $30 million, huge for 1983, but grossed only about $16.9 million in the US and Canada. It's now a cult favorite.
Variety dismissed Krull as a "blatantly derivative hodgepodge" of Excalibur meets Star Wars, but said director Peter Yates' professionalism kept it from becoming laughable.
Freddie Jones, narrating the prophecy as Ynyr, worked in three David Lynch films: The Elephant Man (1980), Dune (1984) and Wild at Heart (1990).
Princess Lyssa's voice isn't Lysette Anthony's. Producers wanted a more mature sound, so American actress Lindsay Crouse secretly dubbed all her lines.
Director Peter Yates made Steve McQueen's Bullitt (1968) and Breaking Away (1979). Krull is his only sword-and-sorcery fantasy.
Columbia president Frank Price asked producer Ron Silverman for a Dungeons & Dragons movie. The first draft was called The Dragons of Krull. D&D's Gary Gygax said nobody ever licensed the game.
Ken Marshall (Prince Colwyn) was 31 during filming. Lysette Anthony, playing his bride Lyssa, was just 18.
Before acting, Freddie Jones (Ynyr) worked as a ceramics-factory lab assistant. He said it nearly drove him clinically insane, and he turned pro in his 30s.
Author Lawrence Watt-Evans disliked the name Glaive. A real glaive is a pole-arm with one long blade, not a "brass starfish".
To promote the wedding, Columbia ran an essay contest. Six couples got married in Krull costumes in 1983. It was dropped because it got no extra press.
Forty Slayer costumes were made for the film, and twenty of them were built in just ten days.
Around 13:00, Colwyn lands on a stone basin and chunks of painted plaster flake off the column, showing the polystyrene underneath.
The Slayers' death shrieks were reused from the Mahar bird-creatures' screams in the 1976 movie At the Earth's Core.
Krull won a Stinkers Bad Movie Award for Worst Picture. Siskel and Ebert gave it two thumbs down, calling it one of the most boring, nonsensical fantasies in a long time.
The film was originally The Dragons of Krull. Richard Scheib of Moria notes it became Krull because there are no dragons in it.
A monstrous snake woman was cut from the script because she looked too much like Medusa in Clash of the Titans, which had come out only a couple of years earlier.
Ken Marshall (Colwyn) modeled his hero on Errol Flynn and did his own stunts, including the mountain climbing. He had just starred in the TV series Marco Polo (1982).
Director Peter Yates also made Summer Holiday (1963), the Cliff Richard bus musical, years before Bullitt's car chase and this space-fantasy.
Krull earned Saturn Award nominations for Best Fantasy Film, Best Music (James Horner) and Best Costumes. Something Wicked This Way Comes took Best Fantasy.
The Glaive pops up as an Easter egg in World of Warcraft, floating out of the lava in the tunnels before the Onyxia boss fight.
Makeup designer Christopher Tucker was first hired to create Krull's creatures but left over creative differences. Nick Maley took over the effects makeup.
Sci-fi author Alan Dean Foster wrote the novelization. Marvel published a comic adaptation by David Michelinie and Bret Blevins.
Krull spawned an arcade game from Gottlieb, a Columbia-owned company, plus Atari and Parker Brothers games. A Krull pinball machine was cancelled, and only ten prototypes exist.
While filming in Italy's Abruzzo region, Peter Yates asked the whole crew to suggest a better title than "Krull". Everyone voted, and the name stayed anyway.
Krull's crew built 23 sets across ten sound stages at Pinewood Studios. Pre-production alone lasted almost a year.
Krull opened on July 29, 1983 in 1,281 US theaters and earned about $5.47 million its first weekend, roughly a third of its entire domestic run.
Ergo's transformations skipped the usual cross-dissolve. Effects chief Derek Meddings blended blow-up stills with artwork. For the puppy, actor David Battley's stills dissolved into a real dog.
Director Peter Yates called his concept for Krull "sort of a fairy storybook that moves," aiming for old-fashioned romance where things were always in motion.
Director Peter Yates released two films in 1983, both for Columbia: Krull and the acclaimed The Dresser, which earned Best Picture and Best Actor Oscar nominations.
The Beast's voice was provided by actor Trevor Martin, who is not credited on screen as the villain.
Liam Neeson and Robbie Coltrane were both early in their film careers when they took supporting roles in Krull.
Robbie Coltrane's voice was dubbed over by an uncredited Michael Elphick, a fellow British actor.
When Ynyr guesses that Torquil has sons, it may have been an ad-lib. Alun Armstrong, who plays Torquil, really does have three sons.
Alun Armstrong (Torquil) spent nine years with the Royal Shakespeare Company. He later originated Thénardier in the West End Les Misérables and won an Olivier for Sweeney Todd.
Bernard Bresslaw, the 6'7" actor playing the Cyclops Rell, wore lifts to look even taller. A radio controlled his single forehead eye, and he could only see out of one eye hole.
Cyclops actor Bernard Bresslaw also played the giant Gort in the 1980 British fantasy Hawk the Slayer.
Nick Maley says the Beast was the first self-contained animatronic suit, with facial, lung, heart and body-fluid movement and no external cables.
The Emerald Seer's glittering cave was built from wood, plaster and glass, with silver glass on the floor. It followed two freezing nights shooting in Black Park near Pinewood.
Production designer Stephen Grimes reportedly modeled the swamp set on photos of World War I battlefield crosses at the Somme.
In the swamp fight at 46:26, a Slayer sinking into the sand is played in reverse. The sand visibly flies upward toward its chest.
The swamp was built on Pinewood's giant 007 Stage, a James Bond stage 336 feet long. The sets took five months to build, and the quicksand was four tons of painted cork.
Ken Marshall (Colwyn) says the swamp shoot was in a very harsh winter. The set was too big to heat, and crew lost in the mist stumbled into "cork chips".
Bernard Bresslaw could only see through one eye hole in his Cyclops costume. During the swamp shoot his fellow actors had to stop him from wandering into the water.
The 2001 PC game Arcanum has a throwing weapon, Azram's Star, modeled directly on the Glaive. Bloons TD 3 also lets Boomerang Monkeys throw Glaives.
Ryan Lambie of Den of Geek called Krull "among the most visually creative and downright fun movies of the enchanted 80s".
Effects supervisor Derek Meddings brought Krull's miniatures expertise from Superman (1978), several James Bond films and Gerry Anderson puppet shows.
The special effects team's quicksand mire swallowed about twenty unlucky technicians at one time or another.
Liam Neeson (Kegan) told Den of Geek in 2011 he's still very proud of Krull and had a lot of fun with director Peter Yates.
James Horner's Krull score was reused as ambient music for Disneyland Paris' Space Mountain: Mission 2.
Composer James Horner reportedly had only about seven weeks to write roughly 110 minutes of music for Krull, while battling illness and a staff shortage.
Janet Maslin of The New York Times called Krull "a gentle, pensive sci-fi adventure" that was a little too moody for the Star Wars crowd.
A shape-shifting "Changeling Claw" hand built for Krull ran out of time and was cut. It was later finished for Tobe Hooper's Lifeforce (1985).
Writer Steve Tesich wrote a second Krull script that was tossed as dialogue-heavy and short on effects. Stanford Sherman's first draft was reused, and Sherman fitted it to the already-built sets.
Jennie Kermode of Eye for Film called Krull "just about the most boring fantasy film ever made." Starburst's Richard Hollis called it "a dull derivative movie idea."
Critic Eric D. Snider wrote that Krull is crammed with magic and quests "yet still manages to be boring... You'd almost have to be doing it on purpose."
In How to Lose a Guy in 10 Days (2003), Matthew McConaughey's character calls his private parts "Krull, the Warrior King".
Family Guy joked about Krull twice. In "Meet the Quagmires" Peter, in 1984, says he'd rather see Krull than Zapped!
An early draft had Lyssa turn villain near the end. Lysette Anthony said she thought that idea was boring, but producers wanted her pure.
A 2007 South Park episode spoofs the Krull Glaive: Jesus uses it to kill self-appointed pope Bill Donohue.
In John Darnielle's novel Wolf in White Van (2014), the reclusive main character buys an ex-rental VHS of Krull and spends four pages musing on it.
Filming began with Ynyr's spider-web climb. Freddie Jones did it without safety wires, because wires would have shown on camera.
Stop-motion animator Steve Archer spent two weeks on the first Crystal Spider model, later redone. It was plexiglass with solid legs, a hollow abdomen and eight black plastic eyes.
Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse director Justin K. Thompson says Krull's spider influenced the Go Home Machine, a spider named Ynyr as a homage.
Francesca Annis' Widow of the Web needed 23 separate aging prosthetic pieces on her face, head and body.
Francesca Annis and Freddie Jones (Ynyr) reunited a year later in David Lynch's Dune (1984).
Robot Chicken spoofed the Glaive's boomerang return: Colwyn throws it in a cave, it jams in his back, and he asks, "The glaive is stuck in my back, isn't it?"
Lysette Anthony told Playboy in 1988 she detests Krull, partly for the dubbing and partly because Princess Lyssa mostly looks helpless and waits to be rescued.
Richard Scheib of Moria gave Krull one star, calling its look a "Saran-wrap world" that feels sterile and lacks any history or culture.
The 2009 comedy Gentlemen Broncos copies Krull's Cyclops and fire mares. One character also gets his dialogue dubbed over, like Lysette Anthony and Robbie Coltrane.
Stunt coordinator Vic Armstrong bought sixteen Clydesdale horses, which trained for months to play the Fire Mares. Horses from the Queen's Household Cavalry were also borrowed.
The "Fire Mares" aren't all mares. Some of the Clydesdales are visibly geldings, and at least one looks like a stallion.
When the horses crossed to France for the Italy shoot, customs needed a passport for each Clydesdale. Each held two photos, a "before makeup" and an "after makeup" shot.
The video game Warframe has characters named Rell and Ergo. Dark Sector's hero also throws a three-bladed Glaive.
Derek Meddings' miniature Black Fortress stood twelve feet high and was lit from within by an electrical system. Lyssa's castle model was twenty feet tall.
Krull was Lysette Anthony's film debut, and the same year she appeared in the TV comedy Auf Wiedersehen, Pet. She later played in Dracula: Dead and Loving It.
Special effects artist Brian Johnson said director Peter Yates hated the shoot so much he vacationed in the Caribbean mid-filming. The effects crew took a three-week break too.
Part of Krull was shot on Lanzarote in the Canary Islands, where Columbia picked the volcanic landscapes of Timanfaya National Park as a backdrop.
In the Black Fortress corridor stunt, Ken Marshall nearly got caught when the floor slabs slammed shut. He says he had no feeling in his heel for months.
Colin Greenland of Imagine magazine said that if as much attention went to the plot as the visuals, "perhaps it wouldn't be so hard to care what happens next."
The Filmtracks review calls Horner's Krull score outstanding but too derivative of his other work of the time, tying it to his Star Trek II and Aliens scores.
Author Lawrence Watt-Evans compared Krull to a superior version of The Dark Crystal (1982), a fairy tale where magic is as ordinary as cars are for us.
Rotten Tomatoes scores Krull at 35% from 26 reviews, and audiences polled by CinemaScore gave it a C+. Its cult following grew anyway.
Filmtracks says the Black Fortress destruction cue has staggered rhythms that could pass for Star Trek II's finale, and the love theme anticipates Horner's The Rocketeer.
RiffTrax spoofed Krull on 28 December 2018, after a RiffTrax Live theater show of it that August.
Screenwriter Stanford Sherman also wrote The Ice Pirates (1984) and the 3D comedy The Man Who Wasn't There (1983), which opened the same year as Krull.
Many of Colwyn's slick one-handed Glaive catches are really throws filmed and played in reverse.
The Krull Glaive shows up in the final battle of Steven Spielberg's Ready Player One (2018), where the character Sho uses it to cut off I-R0k's arm.
At 1:52:12, as the last column of rock lifts away, a long thin rod retracts into the ground near center screen.
Den of Geek's Ryan Lambie praised Krull's harsh climax, noting Star Wars never killed off so many heroes in such a graphic manner.
The Black Fortress was built like a jigsaw puzzle, so its pieces could be pulled apart on cue. The collapse was filmed upside down so the pieces appear to rise into the sky.
The Killstar weapon near the end of Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon is styled very like Krull's Glaive.
In September 2023 it was announced that J.J. Abrams is attached to a Krull reboot.
Because of its poor box office, a Krull sequel was never produced.
